e-3432.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Curve
e-3432.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 +x$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1, 1).$
e-3432.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,1).$  

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,j \\  & =(2x+0+1)\,i+(0+4y+0)\,j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i+4y\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(2(1)+1)\,i+4(1)\,j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we want a unit normal vector, we normalize $\nabla f(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,1)}{‖∇f(1,1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

e-3433.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
e-3433.problem: Consider the plane curve $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0, 4).$
e-3433.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16} - 1,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,4).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)j \\  & =\frac{2x}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{8}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{(4)}{8}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j \\  & =⟨0,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{x-{x}_{0}}=\frac{{v}_{y}}{{v}_{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{y}(x-{x}_{0}) & ={v}_{x}(y-{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(x-0) & =0(y-4) \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the equation of the normal line to the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1$ at the point $(0,4)$ is $x=0.$

e-3434.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface
e-3434.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z) = 2x^2 - xy - z^2,$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$
e-3434.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)$ can be found by computing 
$\nabla f(2, 3, \sqrt 2).$   

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j-2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,3,\sqrt{2}) & =(4\cdot 2-3)\text{ }i-2\text{ }j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k \\  & =5i-2j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $5 \mathbf i  - 2 \mathbf j - 2 \sqrt 2\ \mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$

e-3435.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
e-3435.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z = \ln (x^2 - xy)$ at the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right).$
e-3435.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z) = \ln (x^2 - xy) - z,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2){:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)k \\  & =(\frac{2x-y}{{x}^{2}-xy})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{y-x})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =(\frac{2\cdot 2-1}{{2}^{2}-2\cdot 1})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{1-2})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{3}{2}i-\,j-k \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf v = \langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2)= \left\langle  \dfrac {3} {2}, -1, -1\right  \rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-1} \\ \frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The gradient is ∇f(x,y)=(-y i+x j)/(x²+y²). At (2,-2), it equals (i+j)/4. Normalizing gives (√2/2)(i+j), so option c is a unit normal vector.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-2).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(2,-2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}))i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}))j \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\,i+\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\,j \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j \\ ∇f(2,-2) & =-\frac{(-2)}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{8}\,i+\frac{2}{8}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(2,-2)}{‖∇f(2,-2)‖} & =\frac{\frac{1}{4}(i+j)}{‖\frac{1}{4}(i+j)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}})}\cdot \frac{1}{4}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function f(x,y)=arctan⁡(yx) that passes through the point where (x,y)=(2,−2).

a
22(i−j)
b
i−j
c
22(i+j)
d
i+j
e
22(−i+j)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (x,y)=(2,−2) can be found by computing ∇f(2,−2).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y)=(2,−2):

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(arctan⁡(yx))i+∂∂y(arctan⁡(yx))j=(−yx2)1+(yx)2i+(1x)1+(yx)2j=−yx2+y2i+xx2+y2j∇f(2,−2)=−(−2)22+(−2)2i+222+(−2)2j=28i+28j=14(i+j)

Finally, we normalize ∇f(2,−2): ∇f(2,−2)‖∇f(2,−2)‖=14(i+j)‖14(i+j)‖=1(14⋅12+12)⋅14(i+j)=12(i+j)=22(i+j).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Curve
content.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-2).$
content.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(2,-2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}))i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}))j \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}})}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\,i+\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{1+{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}}\,j \\  & =-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j \\ ∇f(2,-2) & =-\frac{(-2)}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{8}\,i+\frac{2}{8}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(2,-2)}{‖∇f(2,-2)‖} & =\frac{\frac{1}{4}(i+j)}{‖\frac{1}{4}(i+j)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}})}\cdot \frac{1}{4}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The gradient is ∇f(x,y)=(-2y i+2x j)/(x-y)². At (-2,-1), this is 2i-4j, whose magnitude is 2√5. Normalizing gives (√5/5)(i-2j), option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x+y}{x-y}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-2,-1).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(-2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-2,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x+y}{x-y})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x+y}{x-y})\,j \\  & =\frac{1(x-y)-(x+y)(1)}{(x-y)^{2}}\,i+\frac{1(x-y)-(x+y)(-1)}{(x-y)^{2}}\,j \\  & =-\frac{2y}{(x-y)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2x}{(x-y)^{2}}\,j \\ ∇f(-2,-1) & =-\frac{2(-1)}{(-2-(-1))^{2}}\,i+\frac{2(-2)}{(-2-(-1))^{2}}\,j \\  & =2\,i-4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(-2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(-2,-1)}{‖∇f(-2,-1)‖} & =\frac{2\,i-4\,j}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}(2\,i-4\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(i-2\,j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}(\,i-2\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(-2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-2,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x+y}{x-y})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x+y}{x-y})\,j \\  & =\frac{1(x-y)-(x+y)(1)}{(x-y)^{2}}\,i+\frac{1(x-y)-(x+y)(-1)}{(x-y)^{2}}\,j \\  & =-\frac{2y}{(x-y)^{2}}\,i+\frac{2x}{(x-y)^{2}}\,j \\ ∇f(-2,-1) & =-\frac{2(-1)}{(-2-(-1))^{2}}\,i+\frac{2(-2)}{(-2-(-1))^{2}}\,j \\  & =2\,i-4\,j\end{aligned}

$$

$$

after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(5,4).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(5,4)$, can be found by computing $∇f(5,4).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(5,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\text{ }i-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(5,4) & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}\text{ }i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{9}}i-\frac{4}{\sqrt{9}}j \\  & =\frac{5}{3}i-\frac{4}{3}j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(5,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(5,4)}{‖∇f(5,4)‖} & =\frac{\frac{5}{3}i-\frac{4}{3}j}{\sqrt{{(\frac{5}{3})}^{2}+{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{5}{3}i-\frac{4}{3}j}{\frac{\sqrt{41}}{3}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{41}}{41}(5i-4j)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

decision.explanation: ∇g(x,y)=(1/x)i+(1/y)j, so ∇g(1,1)=i+j. Dividing by its magnitude √2 gives (√2/2)(i+j), option d.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,1).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point  where $(x,y)=(1,1)$, can be found by computing $∇g(1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & ={g}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{g}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y\,i+\frac{1}{xy}\cdot x\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j \\ ∇g(1,1) & =\frac{1}{(1)}\,i+\frac{1}{(1)}\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇g(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇g(1,1)}{‖∇g(1,1)‖} & =\frac{i+j}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where (x,y)=(1,1), can be found by computing ∇g(1,1).

So, we first find the gradient of g(x,y) and evaluate it at (x,y)=(1,1):

∇g(x,y)=gx(x,y)i+gy(x,y)j=∂∂x(ln⁡(xy))i+∂∂y(ln⁡(xy))j=1xy⋅yi+1xy⋅xj=1xi+1yj∇g(1,1)=1(1)i+1(1)j=i+j

∇g(1,1)‖∇g(1,1)‖=i+j12+12=22(i+j)

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)={x}^{2}+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,0).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & ={x}^{2}+y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =(-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2x)\,i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,0) & =(-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-2\cdot (-1))\,i+(-(-1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-1)\,j \\  & =2\,i-j \\  & =⟨2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,0)=⟨2,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x+1}{2} & =-y \\ x+1 & =-2y \\ x+2y+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Consider the plane curve ln⁡(x+y)=2xy. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (0,1).

a
x+y−1=0
b
x−y+1=0
c
x+2y−2=0
d
−x+y−1=0
e
x+y+1=0
Submit

decision.explanation: Set F(x,y)=ln(x+y)−2xy. At (0,1), ∇F=(1−2,1−0)=(−1,1), so the normal line has slope −1. Through (0,1), it is y−1=−x, or x+y−1=0.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)=2xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,1).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-2y)\,i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-2x)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(0))\,j \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,1)=⟨-1,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1} & =\frac{y-1}{1} \\ -x & =y-1 \\ x+y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: ln⁡(x+y)=2xyln⁡(x+y)−2xy=0

If we set f(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y)−2xy, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (0,1) can be found by computing ∇f(0,1).

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(ln⁡(x+y)−2xy)i+∂∂y(ln⁡(x+y)−2xy)j=(1x+y−2y)i+(1x+y−2x)j∇f(0,1)=(10+1−2(1))i+(10+1−2(0))j=−i+j=⟨−1,1⟩

Hence, ∇f(0,1)=⟨−1,1⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (0,1).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−0−1=y−11−x=y−1x+y−1=0

verification.explanation: Math Academy declares x+y−1=0, matching option a. Independently, the gradient of ln(x+y)−2xy at (0,1) is (−1,1), so the normal line through (0,1) is y−1=−x, confirming this answer.

content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-2y)\,i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-2x)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(0))\,j \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,1)=⟨-1,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1} & =\frac{y-1}{1} \\ -x & =y-1 \\ x+y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Consider the plane curve 6xy=5x2+y2. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (1,1).

a
x−y+2=0
b
x+y−2=0
c
x+y=0
d
x+y−1=0
e
2x+y+2=0
Submit

decision.explanation: Set F(x,y)=5x²+y²−6xy. Its gradient at (1,1) is (4,−4), so the normal line has slope −1. Through (1,1), it is y−1=−(x−1), giving x+y−2=0.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Consider the plane curve $6xy=5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,1).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,j \\  & =(10x-6y)\,i+(2y-6x)\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(10-6(1))\,i+(2(1)-6)\,j \\  & =4\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨4,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,1)=⟨4,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{4} & =\frac{y-1}{-4} \\ x-1 & =-y+1 \\ x+y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the plane curve x2+y2=2y−x−2. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (0,2).

a
3x+y=2
b
2x−y=−2
c
x−y=−2
d
3x+2y=4
e
x+y=2
Submit

decision.explanation: Set F(x,y)=√(x²+y²)−2y+x+2. Its gradient at (0,2) is (1,−1), so the normal line has slope −1. Through (0,2), it is y−2=−x, or x+y=2.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Consider the plane curve $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=2y-x-2.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,2).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =2y-x-2 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+1)i+(\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2)j \\ ∇f(0,2) & =(\frac{0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}+1)i+(\frac{2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}-2)j \\  & =i-j \\  & =⟨1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,2)=⟨1,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,2).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{-1} \\ x & =2-y \\ x+y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

x−y=−2

x+y=2

EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: x2+y2=2y−x−2x2+y2−2y+x=−2

If we set f(x,y)=x2+y2−2y+x, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=−2.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (0,2) can be found by computing ∇f(0,2).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (0,2): ∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(x2+y2−2y+x)i+∂∂y(x2+y2−2y+x)j=(xx2+y2+1)i+(yx2+y2−2)j∇f(0,2)=(002+22+1)i+(202+22−2)j=i−j=⟨1,−1⟩

Hence, ∇f(0,2)=⟨1,−1⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (0,2).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−01=y−2−1x=2−yx+y=2

verification.explanation: Math Academy declares x+y=2, matching option e. Independently, the gradient at (0,2) is (1,−1), so the normal line through that point is y−2=−x, confirming the result.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Consider the plane curve $\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2}=1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,0).$
after.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(3,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{9}x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇f(3,0) & =\frac{2}{9}(3)\,i+2(0)\,j \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\,i \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{3},0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,0)=⟨\frac{2}{3},0⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-3)0-(y-0)\frac{2}{3} & =0 \\ -\frac{2}{3}y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (3,0) can be found by computing ∇f(3,0).

Hence, ∇f(3,0)=⟨23,0⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (3,0).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

(x−x0)vy−(y−y0)vx=0(x−3)0−(y−0)23=0−23y=0y=0

decision.explanation: ∇f=(y²+2xz)i+(2xy+z²)j+(2yz+x²)k. At (−1,1,−1), this equals 3i−j−k, which is perpendicular to the level surface.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-1,1,-1).$  

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$  and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,k \\  & =({y}^{2}+2xz)\text{ }i+(2xy+{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2yz+{x}^{2})\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,1,-1) & =((1)^{2}+2(-1)(-1))\,i+(2(-1)(1)+(-1)^{2}))\,j+(2(1)(-1)+(-1)^{2})\,k \\  & =3\,i-1j-1\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $3\,i-\,j-\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1).$

a
−3i−j−2k
b
3i−j−2k
c
3i−j−k
d
3i−j−4k
e
i−j−3k
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,1,−1) can be found by computing ∇f(−1,1,−1).

So, we first find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(−1,1,−1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(xy2+yz2+x2z)i+∂∂y(xy2+yz2+x2z)j+∂∂z(xy2+yz2+x2z)k=(y2+2xz) i+(2xy+z2) j+(2yz+x2) k∇f(−1,1,−1)=((1)2+2(−1)(−1))i+(2(−1)(1)+(−1)2))j+(2(1)(−1)+(−1)2)k=3i−1j−1k

Therefore, 3i−j−k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,1,−1).

before.html:
Question 12
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(z2−xy)−yz, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−2,0).

a
i−12j+12k
b
i−2j+2k
c
i−12j+2k
d
i−12j
e
−i−12j+2k
Submit

decision.explanation: ∇f=(−y/(z²−xy), −x/(z²−xy)−z, 2z/(z²−xy)−y). At (1,−2,0), this is (1,−1/2,2), a normal vector to the level surface.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,k \\  & =-\frac{y}{{z}^{2}-xy}\text{ }i+(-\frac{x}{{z}^{2}-xy}-z)\text{ }j+(\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}-xy}-y)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =-\frac{(-2)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}\,i+(-\frac{1}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-0)\,j+(\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-(-2))\,k \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$

Question 12
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(z2−xy)−yz, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−2,0).

a
i−12j+12k
b
i−2j+2k
c
i−12j+2k
d
i−12j
e
−i−12j+2k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−2,0) can be found by computing ∇f(1,−2,0).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(1,−2,0):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(ln⁡(z2−xy)−yz)i+∂∂y(ln⁡(z2−xy)−yz)j+∂∂z(ln⁡(z2−xy)−yz)k=−yz2−xy i+(−xz2−xy−z) j+(2zz2−xy−y) k∇f(1,−2,0)=−(−2)(0)2−(1)(−2)i+(−1(0)2−(1)(−2)−0)j+(2(0)(0)2−(1)(−2)−(−2))k=i−12j+2k

Therefore, i−12j+2k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−2,0).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface
content.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$
content.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,k \\  & =-\frac{y}{{z}^{2}-xy}\text{ }i+(-\frac{x}{{z}^{2}-xy}-z)\text{ }j+(\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}-xy}-y)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =-\frac{(-2)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}\,i+(-\frac{1}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-0)\,j+(\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-(-2))\,k \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(y+5)\text{ }i+x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(-1+5)\,i+(1)\,j+2(2)\,k \\  & =4\,i+j+4\,k\end{aligned}

Question 13
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+z2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2).

a
4i−2j+4k
b
4i+j+4k
c
−4i−2k
d
4j+k
e
i+2j+4k
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2) can be found by computing ∇f(1,−1,2).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(xy+5x+z2)i+∂∂y(xy+5x+z2)j+∂∂z(xy+5x+z2)k=(y+5) i+x j+2z k∇f(1,−1,2)=(−1+5)i+(1)j+2(2)k=4i+j+4k

Therefore, 4i+j+4k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2).

verification.explanation: Math Academy declares 4i+j+4k, matching option b. Independently, ∇f=(y+5,x,2z) evaluates to (4,1,4) at (1,−1,2), confirming this normal vector.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface
content.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=xy+5x+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$
content.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+5x+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(y+5)\text{ }i+x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(-1+5)\,i+(1)\,j+2(2)\,k \\  & =4\,i+j+4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $4\,i+j+4\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,2).$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz},$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,4,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz})\,k \\  & =\frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy}}\,i+(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy}}+\frac{z}{2\sqrt{yz}})j+\frac{y}{2\sqrt{yz}}\,k \\ ∇f(1,4,1) & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{1(4)}}\,i+(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1(4)}}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4(1)}})j+\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(1)}}\,k \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i+\frac{1}{2}\,j+k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1).$

\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{3}yz-xy{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =(3{x}^{2}yz-y{z}^{2})\text{ }i+({x}^{3}z-x{z}^{2})\text{ }j+({x}^{3}y-2xyz)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,1) & =(3(1)^{2}(-2)(1)-(-2)(1)^{2})\,i+((1)^{3}(1)-(1)(1)^{2})\,j+((1)^{3}(-2)-2(1)(-2)(1))\,k \\  & =-4\,i+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-4\,i+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,1).$

decision.explanation: The gradient of √(2x²+y−4z) at (2,1,2) is (4,1/2,−2). Thus the normal line is (x−2)/4=(y−1)/(1/2)=(z−2)/(−2), matching option e.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}=1$ at the point $(2,1,2).$
after.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=1.$     

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1,2).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1,2):$    

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2x}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }j-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,2) & =\frac{2\cdot 2}{\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }j-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }k \\  & =4\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j-2\text{ }k \\  & =⟨4,\,\frac{1}{2},\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-1}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{z-2}{-2} \\ \frac{x-2}{4}=2y-2=\frac{2-z}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16
?

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface 2x2+y−4z=1 at the point (2,1,2).

a
x−24=y−13=2−z2
b
x−22=2y−2=2−z2
c
x−24=y−1=2−z4
d
x−24=2y−2=z−22
e
x−24=2y−2=2−z2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's set f(x,y,z)=2x2+y−4z. Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=1.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (2,1,2) can be found by computing ∇f(2,1,2).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (2,1,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x(2x2+y−4z) i+∂∂y(2x2+y−4z) j+∂∂z(2x2+y−4z) k=2x2x2+y−4z i+122x2+y−4z j−22x2+y−4z k∇f(2,1,2)=2⋅22⋅22+1−4⋅2 i+122⋅22+1−4⋅2 j−22⋅22+1−4⋅2 k=4 i+12 j−2 k=⟨4,12,−2⟩

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0,z0), we get:

x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vzx−24=y−112=z−2−2x−24=2y−2=2−z2

verification.explanation: Math Academy declares (x−2)/4=2y−2=(2−z)/2, matching option e. This agrees with the normal direction ∇f(2,1,2)=(4,1/2,−2).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
content.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}=1$ at the point $(2,1,2).$
content.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=1.$     

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1,2).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1,2):$    

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2x}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }j-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,2) & =\frac{2\cdot 2}{\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }j-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }k \\  & =4\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j-2\text{ }k \\  & =⟨4,\,\frac{1}{2},\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-1}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{z-2}{-2} \\ \frac{x-2}{4}=2y-2=\frac{2-z}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

a
 x−32=y−24=z−1
b
 x−3=y−22=z−1
c

x−1=y−2=z−1

decision.explanation: Set F(x,y,z)=x−y²+z². Its gradient at (3,2,1) is (1,−4,2), so the normal line is x−3=(y−2)/(−4)=(z−1)/2, matching option c.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface x=y2−z2 at the point (3,2,1).

a
 x−32=y−24=z−1
b
 x−3=y−22=z−1
c
 x−3=2−y4=z−12
d
x−1=y−2=z−1
e
 x−14=2−y=z−1
Submit

EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: x=y2−z2y2−z2−x=0

If we set f(x,y,z)=y2−z2−x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (3,2,1) can be found by computing ∇f(3,2,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (3,2,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(y2−z2−x)i+∂∂y(y2−z2−x)j+∂∂z(y2−z2−x)k=−i+2yj−2zk∇f(3,2,1)=−i+2(2)j−2(1)k=−i+4j−2k=⟨−1,4,−2⟩

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0,z0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vzx−3(−1)=y−24=z−1(−2)x−31=y−2−4=z−12x−3=2−y4=z−12

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
content.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)k \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2y)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,-1,1) & =(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\text{ }i+[(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+2(-1)]\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =-i-2\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,-1⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x=\frac{y+1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}

content.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(0,-1,1).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)k \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2y)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,-1,1) & =(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\text{ }i+[(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+2(-1)]\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =-i-2\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x=\frac{y+1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface 4z2−4y2=x2−6x+12 at the point (2,0,1).

a
 ⟨2,0,1⟩+t⟨2,0,4⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
⟨2,0,1⟩+t⟨2,0,8⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
 ⟨2,0,1⟩+t⟨4,−1,8⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
⟨2,0,8⟩+t⟨2,0,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
 ⟨2,0,8⟩+t⟨−1,3,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: Set F=4z²−4y²−x²+6x−12. Then ∇F=(6−2x,−8y,8z), which at (2,0,1) equals (2,0,8). The normal line is therefore ⟨2,0,1⟩+t⟨2,0,8⟩, option b.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}={x}^{2}-6x+12$ at the point $(2,0,1).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-6x \\ 4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x & =12\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=12.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)k \\  & =(6-2x)\,i-8y\,j+8z\,k \\ ∇f(2,0,1) & =(6-2(2))\,i-8(0)\text{ }j+8(1)\,k \\  & =2\,i+8\,k \\  & =⟨2,0,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(2,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨2,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(2,0,1)=⟨2,0,1⟩+t\,⟨2,0,8⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Question 19
?

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface 4z2−4y2=x2−6x+12 at the point (2,0,1).

a
 ⟨2,0,1⟩+t⟨2,0,4⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
⟨2,0,1⟩+t⟨2,0,8⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
 ⟨2,0,1⟩+t⟨4,−1,8⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
⟨2,0,8⟩+t⟨2,0,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
 ⟨2,0,8⟩+t⟨−1,3,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side:

4z2−4y2=x2−6x4z2−4y2−x2+6x=12

If we set f(x,y,z)=4z2−4y2−x2+6x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=12.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (2,0,1) can be found by computing ∇f(2,0,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (2,0,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(4z2−4y2−x2+6x)i+∂∂y(4z2−4y2−x2+6x)j+∂∂z(4z2−4y2−x2+6x)k=(6−2x)i−8yj+8zk∇f(2,0,1)=(6−2(2))i−8(0) j+8(1)k=2i+8k=⟨2,0,8⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(2,0,1) and passes through the point (2,0,1) can be written as

r=⟨2,0,1⟩+t∇f(2,0,1)=⟨2,0,1⟩+t⟨2,0,8⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}={x}^{2}-6x+12$ at the point $(2,0,1).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-6x \\ 4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x & =12\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=12.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)k \\  & =(6-2x)\,i-8y\,j+8z\,k \\ ∇f(2,0,1) & =(6-2(2))\,i-8(0)\text{ }j+8(1)\,k \\  & =2\,i+8\,k \\  & =⟨2,0,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(2,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨2,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(2,0,1)=⟨2,0,1⟩+t\,⟨2,0,8⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(2,0,1) and passes through the point (2,0,1) can be written as

decision.explanation: For f=e^(x+y+z)−2xyz, ∇f=(e^(x+y+z)−2yz,e^(x+y+z)−2xz,e^(x+y+z)−2xy). At (2,−1,−1), this is (−1,5,5). Thus the normal line is (x−2)/(−1)=(y+1)/5=(z+1)/5, matching option c.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface ${e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz=-3$ at the point $(2,-1,-1).$
after.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,-1,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz)k \\  & =({e}^{x+y+z}-2yz)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y+z}-2xz)\text{ }j+({e}^{x+y+z}-2xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,-1,-1) & =({e}^{2-1-1}-2(-1)(-1))\text{ }i+({e}^{2-1-1}-2(2)(-1))\text{ }j+({e}^{2-1-1}-2(2)(-1))\text{ }k \\  & =({e}^{0}-2)\text{ }i+({e}^{0}+4)\text{ }j+({e}^{0}+4)\text{ }k \\  & =-i+5\,j+5\,k \\  & =⟨-1,5,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(-1)}=\frac{y-(-1)}{5}=\frac{z-(-1)}{5} \\ \frac{x-2}{(-1)}=\frac{y+1}{5}=\frac{z+1}{5} \\ 2-x=\frac{y+1}{5}=\frac{z+1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

a
2−x2=y+13=z+1

2−x=y+1=z+1
c
 2−x=y+15=z+15

Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's set f(x,y,z)=ex+y+z−2xyz. Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=−3.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (2,−1,−1) can be found by computing ∇f(2,−1,−1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (2,−1,−1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(ex+y+z−2xyz)i+∂∂y(ex+y+z−2xyz)j+∂∂z(ex+y+z−2xyz)k=(ex+y+z−2yz) i+(ex+y+z−2xz) j+(ex+y+z−2xy) k∇f(2,−1,−1)=(e2−1−1−2(−1)(−1)) i+(e2−1−1−2(2)(−1)) j+(e2−1−1−2(2)(−1)) k=(e0−2) i+(e0+4) j+(e0+4) k=−i+5j+5k=⟨−1,5,5⟩

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0,z0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vzx−2(−1)=y−(−1)5=z−(−1)5x−2(−1)=y+15=z+152−x=y+15=z+15

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
content.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface ${e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz=-3$ at the point $(2,-1,-1).$
content.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,-1,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{x+y+z}-2xyz)k \\  & =({e}^{x+y+z}-2yz)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y+z}-2xz)\text{ }j+({e}^{x+y+z}-2xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,-1,-1) & =({e}^{2-1-1}-2(-1)(-1))\text{ }i+({e}^{2-1-1}-2(2)(-1))\text{ }j+({e}^{2-1-1}-2(2)(-1))\text{ }k \\  & =({e}^{0}-2)\text{ }i+({e}^{0}+4)\text{ }j+({e}^{0}+4)\text{ }k \\  & =-i+5\,j+5\,k \\  & =⟨-1,5,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(-1)}=\frac{y-(-1)}{5}=\frac{z-(-1)}{5} \\ \frac{x-2}{(-1)}=\frac{y+1}{5}=\frac{z+1}{5} \\ 2-x=\frac{y+1}{5}=\frac{z+1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$
